whatYouGet: A complete color/type/spacing token set matching Pandora's blue-navy identity and the exact thumb-state color rules
Production-ready specs for the signature thumb up/down pair, the gradient Now Playing hero, and the station-list row with its equalizer

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who specializes in cloning best-in-class music-app interaction models pixel-for-pixel, then adapting them to a new brand. You have deep fluency in translating a 'genome radio' style thumbs-based recommendation UI into a distinct, ownable design system.
</role>

<reference_data>
Build from these extracted facts about a genome-radio streaming app's iOS interface (do not name the source app in your output; treat these as raw material for a new brand):

Color roles:
- Accent / 'this is on' color: a saturated bright blue used identically for the active thumb-up fill, the circular play button, the scrubber fill, and every primary CTA (roughly #3668FF, pressed state ~12% darker)
- Heritage/deep blue used only for gradient bases and marketing (roughly #224099)
- Dark canvas: a near-navy, NOT neutral gray/black (roughly #0B0F1C), with two lighter surface steps for cards/rows and raised rows
- Hairline dividers roughly one shade above surface-2
- Text: near-white primary, cool blue-gray secondary, darker blue-gray tertiary
- Semantic success/warning/error follow the same cool-blue-tinted logic rather than pure red/green

Typography ladder: a grotesque sans (Inter-class), track title heaviest (~800 weight, ~21pt) so it reads over busy art; station names ~600 weight; body/metadata 400-600; small uppercase eyebrow label with +1pt tracking; all timecodes/counts use tabular lining figures.

Named distinctive patterns to reproduce:
1. Thumb-up/thumb-down pair with a HARD asymmetry rule: thumb-up when active fills solid with the accent color (a permanent, committed vote); thumb-down NEVER fills solid even when active — it stays a hollow/outline stroke in a slightly brighter neutral, because it only skips-and-moves-on. This asymmetry must be preserved in any redesign.
2. A full-screen 'Now Playing' surface with literally NO card frame: the background is a top-to-bottom gradient sampled from the current artwork, dissolving into the dark navy floor, re-derived on every track change with a ~400ms cross-fade. Chrome (top bar, transport) floats directly over the gradient.
3. A calm home list of station/channel rows: square leading artwork, title + subtitle, and a small 4-bar animated equalizer graphic on whichever row is currently playing.
4. A circular primary play button (roughly 66pt) that is the only OTHER solid-accent-filled control besides thumb-up, carrying a soft accent-tinted glow shadow.
5. Corner-radius system: fully square dividers/backgrounds, ~4pt for tiny chips, ~8pt for station art, ~10pt for hero album art, ~12pt for active rows/cards, ~16pt for sheets, full pill (500pt) for buttons/search, true circle for play button and thumb hit-targets.
6. Bottom tab bar with NO active-state pill — active tab is simply a full-opacity text/icon tint change, four tabs, labels always visible.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. The thumb-up/thumb-down asymmetry (solid-when-active up, always-hollow down) is non-negotiable — never let an implementation slip into making both states fill solid, since that erases the 'this is a lasting vote vs. a one-time correction' meaning.
2. Never place a card, panel, or frame around the Now Playing screen — the gradient and floating chrome ARE the design; a bordered container defeats the entire premise.
3. Never tint or color-block directly over album artwork — only the surrounding gradient may sample color from it; the art itself stays untouched and sacred.
4. Reserve the single brand-accent color for exactly four roles — active thumb-up, primary play button, scrubber fill, and primary CTA — so it reads as one consistent 'this is on / do this' signal, never sprinkled decoratively elsewhere.
5. Keep the canvas a deep colored-navy derived from the brand hue, never a neutral gray or pure black — the dark mode must feel like 'this brand, darkened,' not generic dark mode.
6. All timecodes, durations, and vote/thumb counts must use tabular (monospaced) numerals so they never cause layout jitter as they tick upward or downward.
7. Keep the transport row lean — five or fewer large, well-separated controls (skip-down, skip-back, big play, skip-forward, skip-up-equivalent) — never a dense multi-row control panel; this is a lean-back listening app, not an editing suite.
8. Motion stays smooth and unhurried: cross-fades and scale transitions in the 200-400ms range; never snap or bounce aggressively, since the brand personality is calm and focused rather than playful.
9. Never add an active-state pill/indicator behind bottom tab icons — active state is communicated by color/opacity change alone.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / brand: [fill in]
- Primary accent hue (hex or description) and its 'committed vote' semantic meaning: [fill in]
- Base/heritage brand color for gradients and marketing: [fill in]
- Target platform(s): [iOS SwiftUI / also Android / also web]
- Number and names of bottom tabs: [fill in]
- Primary recommendation mechanic (equivalent of 'thumb up/down'): [fill in — e.g. swipe, star rating, heart-only]
- Brand typeface (or say 'use system font'): [fill in]
- Any must-keep legacy UI element from an existing version: [fill in or 'none']
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI Color + Font token extension file matching the reference structure (brand accent, pressed state, navy-derived dark canvas + 2 surface steps + divider, text primary/secondary/tertiary, semantic colors) using the project's actual brand hue.
2. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the signature thumbs-equivalent control pair, explicitly implementing the solid-active/hollow-active asymmetry rule with the exact interaction states (idle, active, tap animation, haptic).
3. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the gradient-hero Now Playing screen: top bar, album art treatment, track text block, scrubber, and transport row, with the artwork-to-canvas gradient logic described precisely enough to implement.
4. The home/station-list row component (or its equivalent) including the now-playing equalizer indicator animation.
5. The full corner-radius scale, spacing scale, and elevation/shadow table adapted to the new brand, following the same philosophy (minimal shadow except for the glow under the primary play button).
6. A motion and haptics table listing every interaction (track change, tap, skip, scrub, tab switch, sheet present) with exact durations/curves and haptic types.
7. A responsive + accessibility checklist covering Dynamic Type exceptions (which text stays fixed for layout), minimum touch targets, VoiceOver copy for the thumbs-equivalent control, and Reduce Motion fallbacks.
</what_to_give_me>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer specializing in premium, content-driven media apps that build their visual identity around per-item dynamic color extraction rather than a single fixed brand palette.
</role>

<reference_data>
Build from these extracted facts about a podcast player's iOS interface (treat as raw material for a new brand, don't name the source):

Color roles:
- Dark canvas is a near-black, NOT pure black (roughly #1A1A1A), with two lighter surface steps and a hairline divider
- One fixed brand accent (roughly #F43E37) used ONLY for tab-bar active state, the primary subscribe-style CTA, and an unread/unplayed count badge
- A SEPARATE 'theme tint' extracted per content-item from its cover art at runtime — this tint (not the fixed brand accent) colors the player's scrubber fill, the circular play button, and any 'active' action chip; it cross-fades (~250ms) whenever the user switches to different content, never a hard cut
- Semantic colors: an info blue for links, a green for played/complete states, a gold for a 'starred/favorited' indicator — all distinct from the fixed brand accent so they never get confused with 'this is the brand'

Typography: the OS native system font family (not a custom brand face) so Dynwamic Type works natively; weight ladder concentrated at 400/500/600/700/800, tabular figures mandatory on every timecode/duration so scrubbing never jitters; uppercase tracked eyebrow style reserved for date-stamps and a 'now playing' label — the only uppercase text in the system.

Named distinctive patterns to reproduce:
1. Per-item theme-tint engine: on opening a piece of content, sample a dominant/representative color from its cover art and inject it (e.g. via SwiftUI Environment) so every descendant view — scrubber, play button, active chips — re-tints live; falls back to the fixed brand accent if the sampled color has poor contrast.
2. Circular geometry as a structural rule: the primary play button, ALL transport controls, list-row play buttons, and the brand mark are circles — never rounded rectangles.
3. A persistent, reorderable 'up next' queue reachable from both the full player and the mini-player, with 'insert next' vs 'insert last' options.
4. First-class playback-effects toggles surfaced directly on the player's action-chip row (not buried in settings) — a 'shorten silences' toggle with named intensity levels, and a 'boost quiet audio' toggle.
5. List rows that pack a date eyebrow, one-line title (never wraps), duration/status metadata, and a trailing circular action button into a compact fixed height, each with a full 44pt+ tap target despite the density.
6. Corner-radius system: 0pt for dividers, ~4pt scrubber track, ~6pt small artwork thumbnails, ~8pt larger cover art and cards, ~12-16pt sheets/modals, full pill (999pt) for every button, true circle for play/transport/avatars.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never confuse the fixed brand accent with the per-item theme tint — the brand accent belongs ONLY to tab-bar selection and the primary subscribe-style CTA; everything on the player (scrubber, play button, active chips) takes the dynamically-sampled tint instead.
2. The dark canvas must be a near-black (like #1A1A1A), never pure #000000 — pure black reads as harsh and loses the subtle surface-step hierarchy this system depends on.
3. Every interactive control that plays, skips, or represents a person/entity must be circular — a rounded-rectangle play button or transport control breaks the brand's core geometric signature.
4. When switching between content items, always cross-fade the theme tint over roughly a quarter-second — an instant hard color swap reads as a glitch, not a feature.
5. Playback-effects toggles (silence-trimming, volume-boosting, or equivalent) must live as first-class chips directly on the player screen, never nested three levels deep in settings — treat them as differentiating features, not obscure preferences.
6. All buttons are full pill radius; nothing in the button system uses a soft/rounded-rectangle shape — reserve rounded rectangles for cover art and cards only.
7. Every timecode, duration, and count must render in tabular (monospaced) numerals so digits never shift horizontally while ticking.
8. Truncate list-row titles to exactly one line with ellipsis; never let a title wrap to two lines in a dense list context — full titles are reserved for the detail/player screen.
9. Keep the app's shadow budget nearly zero except for a theme-tint-colored glow under the primary play button and large cover art — that is the only place 'glow' should appear.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / brand: [fill in]
- Fixed brand accent color: [fill in]
- Content type driving the per-item theme tint (podcast cover, album art, video thumbnail, etc.): [fill in]
- Platform(s): [iOS SwiftUI / also Android / also web]
- Bottom tab names and count: [fill in]
- Signature power-user features to surface as first-class toggles: [fill in]
- Typeface strategy (system font vs custom brand face): [fill in]
- Any existing UI element that must be preserved: [fill in or 'none']
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI Color + Font token file: dark canvas + 2 surface steps + divider, fixed brand accent + pressed state, semantic colors, plus an Environment-based per-item 'theme tint' key with a documented fallback rule.
2. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the Now Playing player showing how the theme tint colors the scrubber, play button, and action chips while the brand accent stays untouched.
3. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the dense list row (date/status eyebrow, one-line title, metadata, trailing circular action) meeting the 44pt tap-target rule despite its compact height.
4. A spec for the reorderable 'up next'-equivalent queue including insert-next vs insert-last semantics and drag-reorder visual feedback.
5. A spec for at least two first-class playback-effect toggles including their row layout, switch styling, and any intensity sub-options.
6. The full corner-radius scale and a motion/haptics table (theme cross-fade, scrubber knob grow-on-drag, swipe-action reveal, reorder pickup/drop) with exact durations.
7. An accessibility pass: which text stays fixed vs scales with Dynamic Type, VoiceOver labels for the play button and list rows, and a Reduce Motion fallback list.

name: Shazam Design System
summary: Rebuild Shazam's single-purpose iOS identification screen: the radial glow gradient, glass surfaces, and the concentric pulse-ring listening animation.
description: A deep-research SwiftUI prompt for cloning Shazam's tab-bar-free hero screen — a radial blue gradient, a single giant central button, and outward-emitting pulse rings while listening.

Production specs for the giant central action button, its concentric pulse-ring listening state, and the springing result-card reveal

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS interaction designer and SwiftUI engineer who specializes in single-purpose 'instrument' apps — interfaces built around exactly one dominant action, where the entire screen exists to serve one button.
</role>

<reference_data>
Build from these extracted facts about a song-identification app's iOS interface (treat as raw material for a new brand, don't name the source):

Color roles:
- The hero canvas is NOT a flat color — it's a radial gradient blooming from a brighter core hue (roughly #0050FF) outward through a mid brand-blue (roughly #0088FF) into a near-black edge/void tint (roughly #08090E)
- All surfaces are translucent glass, not opaque panels — roughly 8% white overlay for resting cards, 14% for pressed/sheet backgrounds, 12% white hairline dividers
- Primary text is white; secondary text is a cool periwinkle tint (roughly #B8C4FF) deliberately chosen to harmonize with the blue gradient rather than reading as flat gray
- A single small warm accent (like a partner-brand pink, roughly #FA243C) appears ONLY on one specific outbound-link affordance, never elsewhere
- Depth/elevation is expressed through blue-tinted glow shadows, never neutral gray drop shadows

Typography: a geometric sans with rounded warmth, only two weights used (500 and 700) — medium for body/secondary text, bold for anything that matters; generous letter-spacing on all-caps eyebrow labels; negative tracking reserved for large result titles only.

Named distinctive patterns to reproduce:
1. NO bottom tab bar at all — this is a deliberate, defining absence. Navigation is just the hero button, a top-left icon, a top-right icon, and an upward-draggable bottom sheet for history/library.
2. A single giant circular action button (~130pt+ diameter) as the dominant, centered object on the entire screen — nothing else competes with it visually.
3. Idle state: the button has a slow, subtle breathing pulse (scale oscillating ~1.0 to ~1.04 over ~2.4s, looping).
4. Active/listening state: 3 concentric rings continuously emit outward from the button — each ring scales up roughly 2.6x its start size while fading opacity from ~0.22 to 0, with a new ring launching roughly every 0.6s so multiple rings are always mid-animation; a soft blue glow also blooms around the button while active.
5. On successful match, the rings collapse, the button shrinks/moves toward the top, and a result card springs up from the button's former position (spring physics, roughly 0.45s, high damping) showing the identified content's artwork as the visual anchor.
6. On failure to match, a single soft horizontal shake plus a distinct error-type haptic — no rings, no card.
7. A bottom sheet with native-feeling drag detents (peek / half / full) reveals a chronological history list once dragged up.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never add a bottom tab bar — the entire premise of this design is a single-purpose hero screen; introducing tab navigation dilutes the one-button identity that defines the brand.
2. The canvas must always be a radial gradient (bright core through mid-hue to a near-black edge), never a flat solid color fill — the glow-from-a-center-point effect is the visual signature, not decoration.
3. Every card, sheet, and panel must be translucent glass (a low-opacity white overlay with a subtle hairline border) so the background gradient is always faintly visible through it — an opaque panel breaks the 'floating in a glowing void' feeling.
4. Secondary/metadata text must use the tuned periwinkle tone, never plain gray — plain gray fights the blue gradient instead of harmonizing with it.
5. Depth and elevation come from colored glow shadows tied to the brand hue, never neutral gray drop shadows — a gray shadow looks like a mistake floating over a colored gradient.
6. The concentric pulse-ring interaction is the single most important animation in the app — implement it exactly as specified (outward scale + fade, staggered launches) rather than substituting a generic spinner or waveform.
7. Limit typography to exactly two weights — one medium, one bold — resist the temptation to add a light or black weight; the restraint is part of the brand's confidence.
8. Keep the hero screen's whitespace maximal — one button, one short prompt line, and vast empty gradient; do not add banners, counts, or secondary CTAs to this screen under any circumstance.
9. On a failed/no-result state, respond with a single restrained shake and a distinct 'error' haptic — never a big red error banner or modal that competes with the button.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / brand: [fill in]
- Core single action this app performs (the equivalent of 'press button, identify audio'): [fill in]
- Brand hue for the radial gradient core: [fill in]
- Any secondary partner-brand color that must appear (e.g. an outbound link to a partner service): [fill in or 'none']
- Platform(s): [iOS SwiftUI / also Android / also web]
- What the bottom sheet should reveal (history, library, settings, etc.): [fill in]
- Typeface (or 'use system font'): [fill in]
- Any must-keep legacy UI element: [fill in or 'none']
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI Color + Font token file implementing the radial gradient (core/mid/edge stops), the translucent-glass surface levels, and the periwinkle-tuned secondary text.
2. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the giant central action button in all three states: idle-breathing, active-listening-with-pulse-rings, and pressed/tap-down — including the exact ring animation timing.
3. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the result-reveal card (glass card, artwork, title/subtitle, primary outbound CTA, secondary glass action row) including the spring-up transition from the button's position.
4. A spec for the draggable bottom sheet with its detents, grab handle, and the chronological history row layout.
5. The full corner-radius scale (circle for the button/rings/avatars, full pill for all buttons/chips, comfortable radius for cards and sheet corners) and the glow-based elevation table.
6. A motion and haptics table covering idle breathing, ring emission, tap-down, result-reveal spring, and the no-match shake, with exact durations/curves/haptic types.
7. An accessibility and responsive pass: which elements stay fixed size across Dynamic Type, minimum/actual touch target for the hero button, portrait-lock rationale, and Reduce Motion fallback for the pulse rings.
</what_to_give_me>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who specializes in audio-social platforms where the waveform visualization itself becomes the primary interactive surface, replacing conventional progress bars entirely.
</role>

<reference_data>
Build from these extracted facts about an audio-sharing platform's iOS interface (treat as raw material for a new brand, don't name the source):

Color roles:
- Exactly ONE saturated brand accent (roughly #FF5500) used identically in both light and dark mode for: the primary play button, the played/filled portion of every waveform, the active tab icon, the 'liked' and 'reposted' active states, and progress indicators — there is no second brand hue anywhere
- A lighter tint of the same hue (roughly #FF7700) is used only for the UNPLAYED portion of a waveform, at reduced opacity
- Light canvas is pure white with a soft light-gray surface for cards/rows; dark canvas is a near-black (roughly #1A1A1A, not pure black) with a slightly lighter surface step — only canvas/surface/divider/text invert between themes, the accent orange stays byte-identical in both
- Text: a dark charcoal (not pure black) primary on light / white primary on dark, with a mid-gray secondary shared across both themes for metadata

Typography: a no-nonsense grotesque, weights concentrated at 400/500/700 only, tabular figures mandatory for every timestamp and play-count so scrubbing/ticking numbers never shift horizontally; all-caps tracked labels reserved specifically for system status tags (like 'reposted' or 'promoted').

Named distinctive patterns to reproduce:
1. The waveform IS the scrubber/progress-bar/comment-timeline all at once — rendered as a dense field of thin vertical amplitude bars. The portion left of the playhead fills solid in the brand accent; the portion right of the playhead uses the lighter tint at reduced opacity. This completely replaces any generic linear progress bar anywhere audio plays.
2. Small circular commenter avatars are pinned directly onto the waveform's baseline at the EXACT timestamp a comment was left; as playback's position-indicator sweeps past one, that comment's text fades in above the waveform for a few seconds, then fades out.
3. A compact miniature version of the same waveform appears inside every track row in feeds/lists (not just the full player), reinforcing the pattern everywhere audio appears, however small.
4. A dedicated 'repost'-style social action (distinct from a simple 'like') that, when active, tints its icon and count in the brand accent and adds a small uppercase status tag to that item wherever it appears in a feed.
5. Buttons use a SLIGHTLY rounded rectangle corner (roughly 4pt radius) — deliberately NOT a full pill shape — this is a specific brand signature distinguishing it from most other music-app button geometry.
6. A persistent mini-player bar above the tab bar carries a thin (2pt) accent-colored progress line pinned to its very top edge as the one always-visible progress cue even when collapsed.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never render a generic linear/rectangular progress bar anywhere audio is playing — the waveform (with its played/unplayed fill split) always takes that role, at whatever scale fits the context (full-size on the player, miniature on list rows).
2. There is exactly one brand accent color in this entire system — never introduce a second 'complementary' hue; all social/action states (like, repost, active tab, progress) share the identical accent value.
3. Keep the brand accent color byte-identical between light and dark mode — only the canvas, surface, divider, and text colors are allowed to invert; the accent itself never adjusts for theme.
4. Buttons use a modest ~4pt corner-rounding, never a full pill (999pt) radius — this slight-rounding is a deliberate, distinguishing brand signature and must not be 'improved' into a pill shape.
5. Pin social/comment markers to their exact audio timestamp on the waveform's baseline — never collect comments into a separate disconnected list without also anchoring them visually to the moment they refer to.
6. Every timestamp, duration, and play/view count must render in tabular (monospaced) numerals so digits never cause horizontal jitter.
7. Keep drop shadows very subtle on the light theme (low opacity, shallow blur) — this app does not use heavy card lift; on dark theme, express elevation via a surface color step instead of a shadow at all.
8. The waveform's progress sweep must advance strictly linearly with playback time — never ease or ease it in/out, since it is meant to be read as a literal clock, not a decorative animation.
9. Reserve all-caps tracked text exclusively for short system-status tags (like a 'reposted' badge) — never use all-caps for a regular section header or button label.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / brand: [fill in]
- Single brand accent color (hex): [fill in]
- Content type carrying the waveform (music tracks, voice recordings, podcasts, etc.): [fill in]
- Platform(s): [iOS SwiftUI / also Android / also web]
- Social actions beyond play (like, repost/share, comment, etc.): [fill in]
- Bottom tab names: [fill in]
- Typeface (or 'use system font'): [fill in]
- Any must-keep legacy UI element: [fill in or 'none']
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI Color + Font token file for both light and dark themes, demonstrating that the single brand accent stays identical while canvas/surface/text invert.
2. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the commentable waveform: bar rendering, played/unplayed fill split, drag-to-seek gesture, and pinned timestamp-avatar markers with their fade-in/out comment reveal.
3. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the track/feed row showing the compact miniature waveform variant alongside title/uploader metadata.
4. A spec for the repost-equivalent social action including its icon states, count display, and the resulting feed status tag.
5. The full corner-radius scale (confirming the ~4pt button rule vs. the sheet/card radii) and an elevation table showing the light-shadow / dark-surface-step split.
6. A motion table covering the waveform's linear progress sweep, the inline-comment fade timing, like-tap bounce, and the mini-bar-to-full-player expansion transition.
7. An accessibility and responsive pass: Dynamic Type exceptions (which text stays fixed), minimum touch targets for the waveform drag surface and action icons, and portrait-lock rationale.

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer specializing in dark, content-forward streaming apps where cover art supplies nearly all of the interface's color and a single brand hue is reserved strictly as a 'verb', never as decoration.
</role>

<reference_data>
Build from these extracted facts about a music-streaming app's iOS interface (treat as raw material for a new brand, don't name the source):

Color roles:
- Canvas is a near-black (roughly #121212) — deliberately NOT pure #000000, because pure black flattens the dynamic gradient effect on the player screen
- One brand accent green (roughly #1DB954, with a slightly lighter logo-only variant and a darker pressed state) is reserved ONLY for: the primary play/follow CTA, the 'liked'/downloaded checkmark state, and equivalent active toggles — it explicitly does NOT appear as the active tab-bar color (that's plain white) and never as body/link text color
- On the accent-green CTA button, the label text is intentionally rendered in near-black, not white — a deliberate high-contrast choice rather than the expected white-on-color default
- Two darker surface steps above canvas for cards and sheets, plus a subtle third 'pressed' surface tone
- Text: white primary, a mid-gray secondary for metadata, a darker gray tertiary for disabled/low-emphasis
- The Now Playing screen's background is NOT a fixed color — it's a per-track dynamic vertical gradient computed by extracting the dominant color from the current album art and fading it into the near-black canvas

Typography: a custom geometric-humanist sans with two optical sizes (a tighter 'UI' cut for small text, a more open 'Title' cut for large text, switching around an 18pt threshold), weights concentrated at 400/600/700 only, negative tracking capped modestly on titles, tabular figures for anything time-based.

Named distinctive patterns to reproduce:
1. Horizontal 'shelves' of square 1:1 album/playlist tiles that scroll sideways, always ending with the last tile 'peeking' half-visible at the trailing edge to signal there's more content to scroll.
2. A currently-playing track row swaps its title/artist text color to the brand accent green AND grows a small animated 3-bar equalizer graphic in place of/beside its thumbnail — this is the only place accent-colored TEXT is allowed.
3. The large circular primary play button (up to ~72pt) uses the brand accent fill with a near-black glyph (matching the CTA contrast rule above), NOT a white glyph.
4. Album/cover art gets only a very slight corner-rounding (roughly 6pt) — enough to soften it but never enough to compromise its square integrity; this is treated as a hard ceiling, not a suggestion.
5. A persistent mini-player bar sits directly above the bottom tab bar whenever anything is playing, expanding into the full player via a shared-element transition where the album art visually 'grows' from the mini-bar's small thumbnail into the full-screen centered artwork.
6. Search input fields are rendered as a light/white field even though the rest of the app is dark — an intentional light-on-dark inversion for the one text-entry moment.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. The single brand accent is a verb, not a decoration — it belongs ONLY on the primary play/follow CTA, the liked/downloaded active state, and the currently-playing equalizer/text treatment; it must NEVER become the active tab-bar indicator color (that stays plain white) and never a link or body-text color.
2. On any accent-colored CTA button, render the label text in near-black, not white — this is a deliberate, specific contrast choice that must be preserved exactly, not 'corrected' to white-on-color.
3. The canvas must be a near-black like #121212, never pure #000000 — pure black flattens the dynamic per-track gradient effect that the Now Playing screen depends on for its sense of depth.
4. Album and cover art gets only very slight corner-rounding (a few points) — never round it enough to look like a typical rounded-rectangle card; the square silhouette must stay recognizable.
5. The Now Playing screen's background must be computed dynamically per track from the album art's dominant color, fading into the near-black canvas — never a fixed static gradient or solid color on this screen.
6. Give every horizontal content shelf a 'peeking' final tile (partially cut off at the trailing edge) so the eye understands there's more to scroll — a shelf that ends flush at the screen edge reads as complete when it isn't.
7. Limit type weights to exactly three values (regular/semibold/bold) — never introduce a thin or black weight, which would undercut the confident-but-restrained voice of the system.
8. Keep the mini-player bar visible above the tab bar at all times during active playback — never let it disappear behind a screen transition, since persistent awareness of 'something is playing' is core to the experience.
9. Reserve large display-size type for nothing — there are no hero headlines in this system, because album art is always the visual headline; text stays in a supporting, moderate size range even on the most prominent screens.
</house_rules>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who specializes in austere, editorial-grade audiophile/premium apps where restraint itself is the luxury signal — radical flatness, true black, and a single meaning-loaded accent color.
</role>

<reference_data>
Build from these extracted facts about a premium/audiophile music app's iOS interface (treat as raw material for a new brand, don't name the source):

Color roles:
- Canvas is TRUE pure black (#000000) — not a softened near-black like other dark-mode apps use; this is a deliberate 'OLED void' choice, not an oversight
- White is the ONLY action color — primary play button, active states, favorited/liked, active tab — used almost like a monochrome-photography aesthetic
- Exactly ONE chromatic accent, a bright cyan (roughly #00FFFF), reserved EXCLUSIVELY for a specific narrow purpose: signaling a premium quality/fidelity tier (e.g. a 'lossless' or 'high-res' badge) — it must NEVER appear on a play button, a like/favorite icon, or an active tab, because that would dilute its single meaning
- Two barely-lifted surface steps above pure black (roughly #0A0A0A and #1A0A0A-range) communicate hierarchy via TONE rather than elevation/shadow
- Secondary text is a cool mid-gray, tertiary an even darker gray

Typography: a geometric/mechanical grotesque, weights concentrated at 400/600/700, tight negative tracking on display sizes, an uppercase +1pt-tracked style reserved specifically for the quality-tier badge text, tabular figures for all durations/track-numbers.

Named distinctive patterns to reproduce:
1. A quality-tier badge (a compact pill or bracket-framed label showing something like a codec/format name) rendered ONLY in the cyan accent with a thin cyan hairline border and transparent fill — this badge appears on track rows, overlaid on album tiles, inline beside a Now Playing title, and in a dedicated quality-detail sheet. It is the single most important visual signature and must appear everywhere fidelity information exists.
2. Album art is NEVER rounded — zero corner radius, always a perfect square, treated as a hard 'no exceptions' rule reinforcing an editorial/hardware-like aesthetic.
3. RADICAL flatness — the entire app uses essentially zero drop shadows anywhere, including on the centered Now Playing album art itself; hierarchy is expressed purely through the tonal surface steps (black → step 1 → step 2). The only shadow exception is a single bottom-sheet lift.
4. The Now Playing screen's backdrop is a full-bleed, heavily-darkened, blurred crop of the CURRENT track's art (not a color-extraction gradient like some competitors) — kept deliberately monochrome-dark rather than colorful, for editorial restraint.
5. Every screen and player transition uses a plain crossfade — no slide, no spring, no bounce, anywhere in the system. This is a strict motion-language constraint.
6. Gallery-like generous negative space — fewer items per screen than typical competitor apps, with deliberately more empty void surrounding each piece of content.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. The single cyan accent means exactly one thing — premium/lossless quality tier — and must NEVER be used for a play button, a favorite/like icon, an active tab, or any other 'this is on' state; those are all plain white. Confusing the two meanings is the single worst mistake possible in this system.
2. The canvas is true pure black (#000000), never softened toward a near-black gray — the OLED-void aesthetic depends on the harshest possible black.
3. Album art (and any tile/thumbnail derived from it) gets ZERO corner radius, always — a rounded corner on artwork anywhere in this system is a defect, not a stylistic variation.
4. This app is radically flat — do not add a drop shadow to ANY element, including the centered Now Playing album art, except the one sanctioned bottom-sheet lift; express all hierarchy through tonal surface steps instead.
5. Never extract a color gradient from album art for backdrops — keep the Now Playing backdrop a darkened, blurred, strictly monochrome crop of the art, resisting the urge to add competitor-style dynamic color.
6. Every transition (screen push, player expand/collapse, track change) is a plain opacity crossfade — banning spring physics, bounce, and slide transitions entirely is a deliberate constraint, not an oversight to 'fix' with more delightful motion.
7. Give the grid and lists generous negative space — resist the instinct to pack in more tiles per row or tighten row height; the void around content is part of the premium signal.
8. Weight the typography ladder at exactly 400/600/700 — no thin, no black — and reserve the uppercase +1pt-tracked treatment specifically for the quality badge, never for a generic section header.
9. There is no light mode in this system — do not design or offer a light theme; the pure-black identity is non-negotiable across the entire app.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / brand: [fill in]
- The single accent color (hex) and precisely what it signals: [fill in]
- What the 'quality tier' badge communicates in your domain (e.g. lossless audio, verified authenticity, pro-grade export): [fill in]
- Platform(s): [iOS SwiftUI / also Android / also web]
- Bottom tab names: [fill in]
- Typeface (or 'use system font'): [fill in]
- Any must-keep legacy UI element: [fill in or 'none']
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI Color + Font token file: true-black canvas, two tonal surface steps, the single cyan-equivalent accent with its pressed state, white-only action colors, and the full text hierarchy.
2. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the quality-tier badge in all four contexts it must appear (track row, tile overlay, inline-with-title, and a dedicated detail sheet).
3. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the square (0pt-radius) track row and album tile, including the currently-playing equalizer state in white (never cyan).
4. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the full-bleed darkened-backdrop Now Playing screen with NO shadow under the centered album art.
5. The complete corner-radius scale (confirming 0pt for all art) and an explicit 'shadow budget' table listing the one sanctioned shadow exception and banning all others.
6. A motion table proving every transition is a crossfade — screen push, player expand/collapse, track change, tab switch — with no spring/bounce/slide anywhere, plus exact crossfade durations.
7. A responsive + accessibility pass: which text/badges stay fixed size under Dynamic Type, minimum touch targets, portrait-lock rationale, and how negative space should adapt across device sizes without ever feeling emptier by mistake vs. by design.
</what_to_give_me>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer specializing in media apps that combine two content formats (audio and video) behind one seamless player, and that carry a strict brand-family typography and color inheritance from a larger parent product ecosystem.
</role>

<reference_data>
Build from these extracted facts about a video-platform-affiliated music app's iOS interface (treat as raw material for a new brand, don't name the source):

Color roles:
- Canvas is an extremely near-black (roughly #030303) — deliberately darker than typical competitor dark-mode apps, specifically so a blurred backdrop glow reads as light emanating from content rather than as a flat panel
- A single saturated red brand accent (roughly #FF0000) exists ONLY as brand chrome: the logomark, a subscribe/premium CTA, explicit/new content badges, and — notably — the scrubber ONLY turns this red while the user is actively dragging it (white at rest)
- Critically, the PRIMARY PLAY BUTTON IS WHITE WITH A BLACK GLYPH, never red — this is a deliberate, explicit inversion of the 'brand color = primary button' pattern found in most apps, and must be called out as a hard rule
- Two dark surface steps for cards/rows, a distinct chip-background tone for filter pills, and family-inherited grey text tones (a lighter secondary grey, a darker tertiary grey) carried over from a parent product's existing design language for brand-family consistency

Typography: the platform's own house/system typeface (never substituted for a competitor's custom brand font), an unusually heavy 900-weight used specifically for top-level screen titles (heavier than most competitors' boldest weight), 700 for section heads, 500 for list rows, 400 for body — tabular figures mandatory for all time-based text.

Named distinctive patterns to reproduce:
1. An immersive Now Playing backdrop: a heavily blurred, up-scaled (zoomed-in) copy of the current track's artwork sits full-bleed behind the player at high opacity, fading into the near-black canvas top-to-bottom — this creates a glow effect rather than a flat colored panel, and crossfades to a new blurred image whenever the track changes.
2. A signature two-segment toggle switch (audio-mode vs. video-mode) positioned directly beneath the album art on the player screen — tapping it must morph the player's layout between a square-artwork layout and a full-width 16:9 video layout WITHOUT losing or restarting playback position. This is the single most identifying interactive element in the whole app.
3. The primary play button is white with a black/dark glyph — explicitly NOT the brand accent color — because in this system red is reserved purely for brand/chrome moments (logo, premium upsell, badges), never for the primary action itself.
4. The scrubber fill and thumb are white at rest, but recolor to the red brand accent ONLY while the user is actively touching/dragging it — reverting to white the instant the drag ends. This is the one moment red touches the actual playback controls.
5. An algorithmically-generated 'up next' queue (framed as an auto-generated recommendation radio, not a static user-built playlist) reachable via a swipe-up shelf from the player, never as a separate full-screen destination.
6. Bottom tab bar includes a dedicated short-form vertical video discovery feed as one of its tabs (a TikTok-style swipe-up feed), distinct from the main library/browse tabs.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. The primary play button is white with a dark/black glyph — NEVER the brand red — this single rule is the most important and most frequently gotten wrong; red is chrome/branding only (logo, premium CTA, badges), and using it on the play button breaks the entire color logic of the system.
2. Keep the canvas extremely near-black (darker than a typical competitor's dark mode) — this isn't arbitrary; the immersive blurred-artwork backdrop needs that near-black floor to read as a glow rather than a flat dark panel.
3. The scrubber is white at rest and turns the brand red ONLY while actively being dragged, reverting to white the instant the drag ends — never make it red as a resting/idle state, and never keep it white while dragging.
4. When toggling between the two content modes (e.g. audio vs. video), the player must morph its layout live and preserve exact playback position — never pause, restart, or reset the timeline when the toggle is tapped.
5. Never substitute the house/system typeface for a custom or competitor-style brand font — using the platform's own type face is what visually ties this app to its parent product family, and departing from it breaks that inheritance.
6. The immersive backdrop must be a blurred, scaled-up crop of the CURRENT track's actual artwork, crossfading to a new blurred image on track change — never a flat solid-color panel or a static generic background image.
7. Never add a tint pill or colored highlight behind the active bottom-tab icon — active tab state is communicated by a plain white icon fill against a muted grey inactive state, nothing more.
8. Frame the recommendation queue as a swipe-up shelf attached to the player, never as its own separate full-screen destination — the queue is a companion surface to the player, not an independent app section.
9. Reserve the heaviest available type weight strictly for top-level screen titles — never apply it to body text, list rows, or button labels, where it would read as visually shouting.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / brand: [fill in]
- Parent product family (if this app inherits type/color from a bigger platform): [fill in or 'standalone']
- Brand accent color (hex) and what it's restricted to (chrome-only vs. action): [fill in]
- The two content modes this app toggles between (if applicable — e.g. audio/video, list/map, text/audio): [fill in]
- Platform(s): [iOS SwiftUI / also Android / also web]
- Bottom tab names: [fill in]
- Typeface (system font vs custom brand face): [fill in]
- Any must-keep legacy UI element: [fill in or 'none']
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete SwiftUI Color + Font token file: extremely-near-black canvas, 2 surface steps + chip-background tone, the brand-red-as-chrome-only palette (with its pressed state), white-as-action-color, and the inherited grey text hierarchy.
2. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the immersive blurred-backdrop Now Playing screen, describing exactly how the blur/scale/opacity/fade should be computed and how it crossfades on track change.
3. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the signature two-segment mode toggle, including the exact interaction for morphing layouts without losing playback position.
4. Full component spec + SwiftUI code for the scrubber showing its white-at-rest / red-while-dragging recolor behavior including the thumb size change and any halo/glow effect.
5. A spec for the swipe-up recommendation queue shelf including its header row and list-row layout.
6. The full corner-radius scale and a motion table (toggle morph, backdrop crossfade, scrubber drag recolor, player present/dismiss, tab switch) with exact durations and easing.
7. A responsive + accessibility pass: which text stays fixed under Dynamic Type, minimum touch targets, orientation/rotation rules for each content mode, and a Reduce Motion fallback for the backdrop crossfade and toggle morph.
</what_to_give_me>
